#222. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#220. Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?

Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis

The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.

Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions. His son and daughter also work at Nvidia, with his daughter seen as his possible proxy, but neither appear to have sufficient experience to take the helm.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 as the CFO after working in finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She’s a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia go from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut. People who know her describe Kress as a calming contrast to Huang’s often confrontational style, Reuters reported.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.”

But that sentiment may not be shared by Huang. During a meeting this past summer, the CEO said Kress was “a deer in the headlights” and interrupted her presentation, a person familiar with the comments told the Wall Street Journal. Huang insinuated during that August meeting that Kress was not someone who could help him make decisions.

However, Kress praised Huang in a memo to employees on Thursday, saying she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.

Many investors, analysts and industry sources who spoke to Reuters questioned whether a finance executive could preserve the technological risk-taking that turned Nvidia into an AI chips powerhouse.

“Putting [Kress] in the interim role makes sense to keep the markets calm, but I don’t think she is the long-term visionary that Nvidia needs to continue its current trajectory,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy.

Kress, who said in her memo that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” , will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor.

The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates. Along with Kress, Buck is seen as a possible successor. He has worked at Nvidia since 2004 and in charge of deploying generative AI in partnership with the world’s top AI companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI and more.

Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang.

Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Kress could face congressional questions about the company’s oversight of chip sales involving Chinese military-linked institutions and south-east Asian intermediaries.

In a 2023 interview with an Israeli publication, Kress credited her two young sons with urging her to join Nvidia in 2013 because they knew its chips from their video games.

She became a billionaire in 2025 based on the value of her Nvidia equity, according to media reports, and Forbes said her net worth of $1.2 billion in mid-2026 put her in 32nd place on its list of America’s richest self-made women.

Kress, who holds an undergraduate degree in finance and an MBA, was also named among the 50 most powerful women in business on rankings compiled by Fortune and Forbes magazines in recent years.

Nvidia’s CEO turmoil comes as the company is set to report its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday.

#219. Chris Van Hollen says he will run for Senate majority leader, challenging fellow Democrat Chuck Schumer – as it happened

Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, announced on Thursday that he is challenging Chuck Schumer for the role of Senate majority leader when Democrats regain the majority in January.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement posted on social media. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer, the leader of the Democratic minority in the current Senate, responded less than a minute later in a social media post of his own. “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

The battle pits a progressive Democrat, Van Hollen, against a centrist, Schumer, in the wake of Senate wins for progressive Democrats in Michigan and Maine who were not initially supported by Schumer.

The contest will also present Democratic senators with a choice between two modes of confronting Donald Trump. Schumer is a cautious politician who has been widely criticized by Democratic voters for failing to stand up to Trump. Van Hollen, by contrast, took on the president’s mass deportation effort head on when he visited El Salvador in early 2025 and demanded to check on the condition of Kilmar Ábrego, a constituent who was wrongly deported to the country.

In a friendly, softball interview with the sports pundit Stephen A Smith on Thursday at the White House, Donald Trump defended the Iran war with a big lie, and deflected blame for his party’s midterm losses with misinformation.

On Iran, Trump falsely claimed, as he has repeatedly, that the war he started in February was essential to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

In fact, US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that it was their assessment that “Iran is not building a nuclear weapon” and that the country’s supreme leader at the time, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei “has not reauthorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003”.

Three months after that assessment was written, Trump ordered the US bombing of suspected uranium enrichment sites in Iran, which could be used for peaceful energy purposes or weapons making, and declared in June 2025 that “Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.”

Speaking to Smith on Thursday, however, Trump claimed that the war he started with Iran just eight months later, in February, was necessary because of “the nuclear weapon that they were two weeks away from having”.

There is no public evidence that Iran had restarted the nuclear weapons program it suspended 23 years ago, but the rhetorical device of claiming that the regime was close to having a weapon has been deployed, for three decades, by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

In the same interview, the president also sought to deflect blame from himself for the losses by Republican candidates for the US Senate in at least nine states he visited for campaign rallies in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign: North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Mississippi, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Michigan and Ohio. (He also visited Alaska to campaign for the Republican incumbent, who seems to be on track to lose as well.)

Asked by Smith what happened in the elections, Trump pointed to the candidates and reminded Smith that he won all of those states as a presidential candidate two years ago (before his popularity plummeted as a result of his decision to raise the cost of goods and fuel for Americans by imposing tariffs on imports and then attacking Iran).

He then suggested that he was still popular in all of those formerly Republican states that responded to his rallies by voting to reject the candidates he campaigned for. “I think I still have it,” Trump told Smith. “You saw with the rallies, I mean, the rallies were packed. We’d have 15, 20, 25,000 people at every rally,” he added, repeating a false claim he made at most of those rallies, which were, in fact, held in smaller venues, not all of which were filled to capacity.

In San Antonio, Texas, for instance, a spokesperson for the the venue Trump spoke at, Freeman Coliseum, told reporters the White House requested a three-quarter-house setup, so the hall was set up with 6,844 seats. In Greenville, North Carolina, he spoke to 5,000 people at the Pitt-Greenville Airport a fire marshal told the local News & Observer. In Port Huron, Michigan, he packed a small hockey arena with a capacity of 3,000 people. In Chillicothe, Ohio, Trump claimed that there were 42,000 people in attendance at a university sports center that holds 2,400 spectators.

Taking time out of his busy schedule of posting on social media, Donald Trump sat down for a lengthy podcast interview on Thursday with the sports pundit Stephen A Smith to express sympathy for Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees.

Asked by Smith, a bombastic commentator who has floated the idea of entering politics himself, if Huang should have stepped down, Trump sighed deeply before saying: “Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.”

Trump also defended Huang, who sat at his table at a White House state dinner for China’s president, Xi Jinping, in September as “a tremendous talent”.

“I can tell you this, somehow he’ll end up in his feet,” Trump added. “I mean, I know him; I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.”

“He called me as the president – I’m president – and he called me and he said, ‘What I’ve done to my wife and family is, is- that’s what he talked about,” Trump told Smith.

A return to normal politics: Darline Graham meets with South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews

During the final stretch of South Carolina’s Senate race, Darline Graham laced into her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews, calling her “bat shit crazy,” at a rally with Donald Trump, in what came off as a feeble attempt to match the president’s bravado.

After Andrews’s stunning win, in a seat left vacant by Graham’s late brother, Lindsey Graham, the two appear to be civil.

Democrat Cindy Holscher has been elected Kansas’ next governor, narrowly defeating Republican Ty Masterson to keep the office in her party’s hands and extend a massive wave of Democratic victories across the country.

Democrats had already secured a majority of governorships in US states for the first time in two decades, even prior to the narrow win in Kansas, where Holscher had already declared victory but the Associated Press did not call the race until Thursday.

Holscher, a state senator, promised to halt new data centers and overcame a flood of money that Republicans poured behind Masterson, the president of the Republican-controlled state senate. She will succeed outgoing governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat who was barred from running for a third term by term limits.

Kelly, a centrist Democrat, had opposed the more progressive Holscher in the Democratic primary, and endorsed her rival, state senators Ethan Corson, but campaigned for the party’s nominee in the general election.

In a campaign ad supporting Holscher last month, Kelly described Masteron as an extremist and assured voters the Democrat would “govern from the middle”.

Masterson, who was endorsed by Donald Trump, remains the Kansas state senate’s Republican leader.

Retaining the governor’s mansion was the third in a series of big wins for Kansas Democrats, after Adam Hamilton was elected to the US Senate, defeating the Trump-backed incumbent Roger Marshall, and Chris Mann defeated the state’s incumbent Republican attorney general Kris Kobach.

Kobach has helped sow doubt about US elections and served as vice-chair of Trump’s short-lived commission on election fraud in 2017, when he tried, and failed, to find evidence to support Trump’s baseless claim that he had not lost the popular vote in the 2016 election.

Mann, a former police officer, had narrowly lost to Kobach in 2022.

Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa, said Democrats should be cautious about spending too much time pursuing Trump administration investigations, claiming voters want to see progress, not rehashing of old wounds.

“Every time I read, right now, about more investigations of things that have already been reported on in the media, I’m thinking, why do we need to investigate that? It’s already been reported on. Why don’t you do something actually productive or better people’s lives,” Sand told reporters on Thursday in Denver at the What’s Next conference on the future of the Democratic party.

Sand recalled that while serving in the Iowa State Auditor’s office, the team typically did not pursue investigations that had been fully reported on because the public was already aware of potential corruption or misuse of taxpayer funds.

“I think that’s a pretty simple guideline for people,” Sand said. “Put your time into doing something that’s actually going to improve people’s lives and not just remind them of a bad thing that the other side did.”

Sand, who largely campaigned on a platform of being independent and called for the end of the two-party system, said he’s chosen to come to the What’s Next conference because he liked the organization behind it, Majority Democrats.

“I’m here for a day,” Sand said. “I think it’s important to talk about what we did in Iowa and anytime I can spread the message about making politics, making government, not redder or bluer, but redder and truer, I want to take that opportunity.”

While votes are still being counted in one tightly contested Senate election, the race in Alaska where Democrat Mary Peltola now holds a 3,975 vote lead over the nearest Dan Sullivan – the one who is the Republican incumbent – the outgoing Republican majority in Washington is using its final weeks in charge to stack the federal courts with as many judges nominated by Donald Trump as possible.

The Senate has already voted on Thursday to confirm one conservative, Gregory Cook, to be a US district judge in Alabama, and to move to final votes on Trump’s nominations of two judges he previously installed on the federal bench – Daniel Domenico and Anna St John – to serve on federal appeals courts.

The vote on St John’s nomination began with a flub by the senator presiding over the Senate, Darline Graham, the South Carolina Republican who is still serving out the remainder of her late brother Lindsey’s term, which ends in January, despite losing the seat to Democrat Annie Andrews last week.

Reading aloud from a piece of paper in front of her, Graham called the vote to end debate on St John’s nomination by mistaking the abbreviation for saint in her name, with the one for street. “The question is,” Graham said, “is it the sense of the Senate that debate on the nomination of Anna Street John of Louisiana to be United States judge for the fifth circuit shall be brought to a close?”

The Alliance for Justice (AFJ), a progressive judicial advocacy group, strongly opposed all three nominees.

Cook, who worked as a volunteer attorney in the 2000 Bush v Gore legal battle, is described by the AFJ as “a lifelong conservative who has consistently aligned himself with extremist ideologies in pursuit of more political power” whose “track record demonstrates a commitment to corporate interests and the spread of conservative ideology — not justice.”

Domenico, who is described by the AFJ as a potential supreme court nominee, was nominated to the US district court in Colorado by Trump in 2019. This year, Trump picked him to serve on the US court of appeals for the 10th circuit in Denver.

In January, when Trump nominated Anna St John to serve as a federal judge for the US district court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, the AFJ wrote that she “has spent her legal career silencing women, attacking LGBTQ+ rights, and cutting off corporate accountability for everyday people.” Before being confirmed to that role, and then nominated to a federal appeals court in New Orleans, St John led the Hamilton Legal Law Institute, which the AFJ calls “a far-right extremist organization that routinely files lawsuits to attack civil rights, undermine consumer protections, eliminate gender equality, and deny basic human rights”.

In her confirmation hearing for her elevation the the appeals court in August, St John refused to say that Trump lost the 2020 election and refrained from characterizing the January 6 2021 Capitol riot as an insurrection.

Just about everything he’s done since – from appointing immigration hardliner Stephen Miller his chief of staff to threatening one of the top Democratic investigators – indicates he’s not looking to change much at all. “Billions of Dollars are being stolen on an hourly basis. Hopefully his words will ring true! It will be an honor to work with him on this very big Democrat problem that, when solved, will literally balance the Budget of the U.S.” the president writes.

Little he writes in that sentence appears to be true. There are 8,760 hours in a year, and the Government Accountability Office estimated in 2024 that between $233 bn to $521 bn are lost to fraud annually – so certainly not billions “on an hourly basis,” as Trump wrote. Meanwhile, there are unanswered questions around how Trump has gone about increasing his wealth since he’s been president:

Democrats may have ridden voter concerns over the war with Iran to their largest congressional majority in years in last week’s midterm elections, but Donald Trump today announced that the US is no longer bothering to find peace with its Middle Eastern adversary. Here’s more, from the Guardian’s Andrew Roth:

Donald Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations with Iran, to focus on domestic politics instead.

In a post to his social media site on Thursday, Trump said he was redirecting the vice-president to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S”.

Vance had reportedly been talking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations to end the war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing access to the strait of Hormuz, which led to a steep increase for the cost of fuel around the globe.

But on Thursday Trump appeared to shut down the negotiations, redirecting Vance to focus on domestic issues and downplaying the need for a final deal.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

While many of these inquiries are sure to be strictly partisan affairs, Michael McCaul, an outgoing House Republican who supports defending Ukraine against Russia, just signaled his support for this particular line of questioning, writing the following on X:

double quotation markI am deeply concerned by reports that Ukraine’s access to Starshield has once again been restricted. Donald Trump’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, is facing potential legal trouble after a Democratic senator opened an inquiry into whether the lied to Congress, citing reporting by the Guardian. Here’s more, from the Guardian’s Michelle R Smith:

A top Democratic senator has launched an investigation into evidence that Robert F Kennedy Jr “unlawfully lied” in his 2025 confirmation hearings to become the US health secretary, citing a report by the Guardian.

Ron Wyden of Oregon, the incoming chair of the powerful Senate finance committee, is seeking extensive records from Children’s Health Defense (CHD), the non-profit anti-vaccine group Kennedy has used as a vehicle to fuel his political rise, including all documents related to a 2019 trip Kennedy took to Samoa.

“We are beginning an investigation into evidence that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy, Jr unlawfully lied to Congress on multiple occasions,” Wyden said in a letter to the group that was sent on Wednesday and obtained by the Guardian. The letter was also signed by Angela Alsobrooks, a Democratic senator from Maryland.

In the letter, the two lawmakers cited reporting by the Guardian that indicated Kennedy lied about his reasons for going to Samoa in 2019, a trip that occurred just months before a measles outbreak killed 83 people in the Pacific island nation, mostly children under age five.

The trip, which Kennedy made as the chair and chief legal counsel of CHD, became one of the most criticized events in his career before he entered government. Critics, including Samoan officials, have said Kennedy’s presence emboldened anti-vaccine activists in Samoa, worsening a vaccination crisis. Kennedy has denied the allegations, saying he never gave any public statement about vaccines or discouraged Samoans from getting vaccinated.

The Trump administration faces an investigation of its scheme to take a 15% cut from any Nvidia chip sales going to China, as part of a deal to secure export licenses for the semiconductors.

Under the scheme, Nvidia chips made in Taiwan could be sold to Chinese companies if they were imported to the US first for a security review. This also made them subject to a 25% tariff under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which was aimed at dealing with imports that threaten national security. The commerce secretary could then grant an export licence to sell the chips to China.

Two Democratic senators are now demanding Trump officials retain all records relating to the scheme as the fallout from now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy continues to grow.

Senate finance committee ranking member Ron Wyden and House ways and means committee ranking member Richard E. Neal said they were beginning to investigate following reports of the affair – which led to Huang’s resignation on Thursday. One focus of the investigation appear to be report that both commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Donald Trump were briefed about the relationship but granted export approvals anyway.

double quotation markThe Trump administration’s ostensible attempt to mask an unconstitutional export tax as a national security tariff action – benefitting both Nvidia and the Chinese government – raises serious concerns within our committees’ jurisdiction over matters relating to taxation and tariffs.

Congress wrote Section 232 to give the president a tool to take action against imports he has determined to pose a national security threat; Trump’s use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk.

#218. Canadian Authorities Kill 4 Bears Involved in Deadly Attack on Hikers

Wildlife authorities said evidence, including animal DNA, conclusively linked a sow and her three cubs to the deaths of two women along a hiking trail in British Columbia.

Four grizzly bears were responsible for the attack that killed two women in British Columbia this month, the wildlife authorities in the Canadian province said on Tuesday.

The sow and her three cubs were captured over the weekend and forensic testing, including the examination of animal DNA, conclusively linked them to the attack, the provincial Conservation Officer Service said. The investigation found that the attack likely involved predatory behavior, and the bears were put down to protect public safety, the service added.

The remains of the two victims, who were identified by their family as Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed, were found along a hiking trail near Bella Coola, a small coastal community northwest of Vancouver. One of Ms. Balcarras’s brothers told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that she and her daughter were familiar with the trail and had been out for “a casual walk.”

The two women went hiking on Saturday, Oct. 31, and were reported missing the next day, according to the broadcaster. The authorities said the first victim’s remains were found on Monday, and the second’s on Tuesday.

The discovery of the women’s remains set off a dayslong investigation to determine what happened to them. The wildlife authorities said on Tuesday that more than a dozen officers were involved in gathering evidence and working in difficult terrain and weather to capture the bears.

The area is home to a large population of grizzly bears, but the authorities said fatal attacks by the animals involving predatory behavior are rare.

Last November, a grizzly bear severely mauled three children and an adult on a school trip. That attack occurred about two miles from the site of the deaths this month. The authorities did not capture that animal but they were able to collect its DNA. Testing confirmed that the four bears captured and killed this month were not involved in the attack last year, the wildlife authorities said.

In response to the deaths, the Nuxalk Nation, the Indigenous governing body in Bella Coola, said last week that it was recommending an 8 p.m. curfew for residents. It also said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was conducting night patrols and escorting students from the school bus.

That curfew has been lifted following the capture of the four bears, Samuel Schooner, the elected chief councilor of the body, said in a statement. The night patrols will continue and will be reassessed in the coming days, he added. Mr. Schooner urged the community to remain vigilant and report any bear sightings to the authorities.

The Conservation Officer Service said in its statement on Tuesday that it will conduct further analysis to determine the circumstances that led to the deadly attack.

Qasim Nauman is a Times editor in Seoul, covering breaking news from around the world.

#217. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#213. On Dakar’s Packed Beaches, Africa Welcomes Its First Youth Olympics

The 2026 Youth Olympic Games are taking place in Senegal, where the beaches and streets are teeming with sports fans and fitness fanatics.

The 2026 Youth Olympic Games are taking place in Senegal, where the beaches and streets are teeming with sports fans and fitness fanatics.

Skateboarding in Ngor, a neighborhood of Dakar, Senegal’s coastal capital. Fitness and athletic prowess are all-important in Dakar. Credit...

Ruth Maclean and Ricci Shryock reported from the beaches of Dakar, Senegal, where it seemed as though they were the only ones not exercising.

Teenage athletes from all over the world have descended on Senegal this month to compete in Africa’s first ever Olympic events, the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

And in Dakar, Senegal’s sports-crazy capital on Africa’s westernmost tip, the locals are ready.

Fitness and athletic prowess have long been all-important here in Dakar. On any given day, ordinary young people put some of the world’s most toned muscles to work, wrestling, skateboarding, surfing and bike riding.

Women toting goggles and foam noodles make their way down alleyways to the sea to take part in mass early-morning water aerobics classes with energetic coaches.

Groups of men do synchronized calisthenics on the city’s public beaches, hopping backward in low frog jumps and coating themselves in fine sand after sets of push-ups.

Weight lifters lift homemade barbells formed by pouring concrete into buckets and sticking a piece of metal into it to dry.

And every evening, crowds gather up and down the city’s main coastal road — the Corniche — to run, lunge, jump and use the many outdoor gyms that have opened in the city in the past decade.

On a recent evening on Koussoum Beach, hulking men tied traditional loincloths around their waists and between their legs. Then they circled each other, pawing at each other’s hands like cats and pulling each other to the ground.

Beach wrestling is making its Olympics debut at the Games, delighting many in Senegal, where traditional wrestling is wildly popular. Traditional Senegalese wrestling has been practiced for centuries here, and in recent years has become extremely popular and lucrative for top-tier competitors.

#212. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang expected to testify before Congress amid calls for crackdown on China chip exports – live

Huang’s resignation has sent shockwaves through the AI industry, after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy

Full report: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO

Analysis: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?

US House Speaker Mike Johnson has said ⁠there is a ​growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US ⁠authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

In the last week, representatives from both sides of the aisle have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips; chips that could underpin China’s surging AI development.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are ⁠widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US ​has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips ‌because it wants its own companies to stay ahead in the race.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told ‌reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach ​new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorisation bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity.

Republican Senator Jim Banks has said that for the last two years, US lawmakers have been pushing to stop America’s “high-end computer chips from being exported to China.”

Banks said he hoped that Jensen Huang would come and testify before Congress.

double quotation markNvidia opposed my legislation a year ago. They opposed other export control laws.

double quotation markWe have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year that would allow some of these issues to continue to occur.

A growing number of lawmakers ​criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist. In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration ‌had held off from adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the trade blacklist.

The US has not posted ‌any additions to that list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. Reuters earlier reported that the US commerce department has not added new Chinese companies to that list for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China.

“Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fuelling China’s military,” Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren said.

Warren, who will chair the senate banking committee starting in January, wrote to Lutnick, secretary of state Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, ‌telling the administration to preserve all documents related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced AI chips to China and related national security risks.

Separately, US Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon and Representative Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrats on the Senate finance committee and House ways and means committee, wrote to Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the administration’s approval of sales of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to Chinese companies “with concerning links to the Chinese government, military, and sanctioned entities.”

The lawmakers also questioned Trump’s decision to grant Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales through a Commerce Department action, which they ⁠called “an unconstitutional export tax.“

Jensen Huang supported more exports to China, despite repeated calls from China hawks in both parties to crack down ​on Beijing’s access to the technology.

Republican Tim Scott – the chair of the US Senate banking committee – has called on Howard Lutnick to testify over the Nvidia scandal, as senior White House officials reportedly mull whether the commerce secretary should be pushed out of the Trump administration.

As the fallout over the loss of one of the AI industry’s most significant figures continues, Lutnick has faced accusations he has not done enough to restrict chip shipments to China.

The ⁠White House and commerce department did not immediately respond to requests for comment after Reuters reported White House officials were discussing Lutnick’s future. Earlier on Thursday, a White House official said ​Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the ‌position”.

The New York Times reported on Thursday that Lutnick has clashed with other Trump officials over how to regulate sales Nvidia’s chips – and that he has faced accusation from inside the administration that his department is “too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang” and failed to “adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China”.

A number of Republicans have gone public with their demand that Lutnick explain his agency’s apparent failure to block Megaspeed – the company linked to Alice Huang – from buying advanced chips. US officials had reportedly started to monitor Alice Huang after suspecting the firm she worked for was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions.

“The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?,” Republican Senator John Kennedy said in an interview on Wednesday.

double quotation markSecretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country. If I were he, I’d call a press conference this afternoon and explain what happened and why he agreed to sell ‘em chips, and I would stop doing it.”

As questions abound about Megaspeed, Singaporean authorities said in a statement on Thursday that Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the centre of the global spy drama had been barred form re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company.

The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” related to Megaspeed, which is registered in the country.

Eventually she was released with a stern warning, but she has been barred from re-entering the country.

Huang was being investigated in Singapore as part of a larger probe into several companies, including Megaspeed.

Singapore police said last October they were investigating Megaspeed over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” after a US senator requested the commerce department investigate whether the firm had diverted Nvidia chips.

In Taiwan, the interior minister told lawmakers on Wednesday that Alice Huang was also now barred from entering the territory.

From a lottery retailer in rural Australia to a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur, and an unexpectedly quiet office in Singapore, as the Nvidia scandal has unfolded more information has emerged about the activities of cloud computing firm Megaspeed, and its former director Alice Huang.

On its website, ​Megaspeed, which is registered in Singapore, describes itself as a Nvidia cloud partner in the Asia-Pacific region.

In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware.

But questions have been raised about the seeming incongruity between its corporate presence and business activities.

Singaporean news outlets, The Straits Times reported that Swiftdata, which owns Megaspeed, has a registered business address that an interior design firm says it has occupied for over four years.

When the New York Times visited Megaspeed’s Singapore headquarters last year, located in the central business district, only two employees were present.

In Malaysia, one of Megaspeed’s offices was reportedly a dilapidated store front in Kuala Lumpur. Another was located in a shopping mall, the Times reported. When one employee emerged in the mall, she was asked what the company did. “It’s not clear,” she responded.

Meanwhile in Australia, Reuters tracked corporate filings of Megaspeed affiliates that led it to a man in his twenties born in Shanghai.

The individual is also registered as director of Megaspeed’s Malaysian, Indonesian and Thai units, according to Reuters.

Unable to contact him, Reuters tracked his home address to a small newsagent and lottery retailer in a regional town outside Melbourne where they found a woman ​who said she was his mother.

The woman said she had run the business for about 16 years, that her son was based in Shanghai and had nothing to do with the Singaporean company.

Some US lawmakers are pushing for a swathe of new legislation that would affect the export of AI chips from America.

The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports.

The Chip Security Act would require companies ⁠to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.

The Match Act would pressure US ​allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced ​chipmaking equipment destined for China.

The Remote Access Security ​Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access ​Nvidia chips.

US representatives from both sides of the aisle have been questioning Donald Trump’s decision to grant Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales.

double quotation markIf you think about the uncertainty that’s created about a potential management change, investors are going to look for alternatives.”

Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.

This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading.

But what makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself.

One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments.

The US Senate banking committee Chair – Republican Tim Scott – has ⁠sent letters to Donald Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, along with Jensen Huang, asking them to testify.

Senior Democrats have said Congress must demand answers from Jensen Huang and Nvidia, after the CEO resigned on Thursday.

Among the questions that need to be answered is what the president knew when he personally invited Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, Schumer said in his social media post on X.

double quotation markAmericans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”

Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been named as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at companies including Cisco and Microsoft. She is a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia’s rise from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut.

“I spoke to him yesterday,” the president continued. “He’s he’s going through hell.”

Flowers were placed outside Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California on Thursday afternoon; an apparent tribute to former EO Jensen Huang.

The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO after the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resigned amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role.

Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.

Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosystem relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn.

The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates.

Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice-president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang.

Donald Trump has reacted to the resignation of Huang by saying Huang “has done a fantastic job,” and adding, “There is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple.”

“A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote on his social media site of Cook, who is Apple’s former CEO.

Donald Trump has reiterated that it is not yet ‌determined whether Alice Huang ‌was a spy.

In an interview released late on Thursday, the President was asked whether Jensen Huang should have resigned.

double quotation markThe big thing is, was the woman a spy? ‌And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet. But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.”

On Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without naming anyone involved.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years.

Blanche said at a ⁠press conference that “of course” the FBI was investigating reports that Alice Huang was working for the Chinese government.

Beijing has ⁠denied Alice Huang is a spy and Huang herself has not spoken publicly.

Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US ⁠authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

In the last week, representatives from both sides of the aisle have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips; chips that could underpin China’s surging AI development.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told ‌reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach ​new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorisation bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity.

Jensen Huang is expected to testify before the US Congress in the next fortnight, after the Nvidia CEO stepped down from the multi-trillion dollar company on Thursday, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shock waves across the global AI industry.

House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony.

Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years.

It has been reported that Jensen Huang also had an intimate relationship with two Nvidia employees, which added to the pressure on Huang, with the company’s board calling a meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the chief executive’s future.

Huang’s exit could have far-reaching consequences ⁠for US chip export policy and the broader AI ecosystem, ​given the ex-CEO’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market as well as his close ties with US president Donald Trump.

Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee, bookending a stunning fall from grace of one of the leading figures of the AI boom. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a successor is named.

Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 14% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced and ricocheted through the global economy, before recovering to finish more than 4% lower as uncertainty about Nvidia’s future leadership troubled investors eased somewhat.

#208. UK ministers look at quick ways to limit NDAs after Walliams allegations

Government considers further curbs on non-disclosure agreements after Guardian investigation of TV personality

Ministers are looking at ways to change the law quickly to expand protections that stop non-disclosure agreements being used to cover up harassment or discrimination in the wake of the allegations about David Walliams.

This could involve extending measures that mean an NDA cannot be used this way to silence an employee so that it also applies to others, such as freelancers or volunteers.

Following an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, which said Walliams used his power and status to prey on young women for sex, there have been reports that NDAs were used by an employer to silence at least one woman connected to him.

Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and a top-selling children’s author, denies any wrongdoing.

The Employment Rights Act bars NDAs being used to stop employees disclosing possible harassment or discrimination, and a recent government consultation looked at the idea of extending this protection more widely.

Such moves are expected to be speeded up after a planned meeting next week between Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, and representatives from TV and film – both of which rely heavily on freelance or contract staff – as well as publishing and sport, to discuss possible new protections.

“We are very much in the space of looking at areas that we can change quickly and without legislation if there are loopholes,” one government official said. “It is still early but extending these protections beyond employees is definitely the sort of thing we are looking at.”

Under other existing legislation, NDAs cannot be used to stop victims or witnesses of crime from giving information to certain specified bodies, for example police or regulators.

Another possible change could extend this protection so that people could speak about crimes to anyone, including the media.

Campaigners had already been pushing for greater safeguards against NDAs before the allegations about Walliams, or the conviction of Russell Brand, who was jailed on Monday for rape and sexual assault.

Zelda Perkins, a former PA to Harvey Weinstein who broke an NDA that barred her discussing the now-jailed Hollywood producer’s predatory behaviour, and has since become a leading campaigner against their misuse, said she hoped the government, led by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), would be galvanised by the Walliams allegations.

“I have great confidence that [DBIST] are trying to create the best possible version of this,” she said. “But extending protections over harassment and discrimination beyond employees is absolutely key, and this is something where we need to keep up the pressure. The last couple of weeks have really highlighted the issues around this.”

Answering questions on Wednesday in the Commons, Nandy agreed with a Conservative question about the need to stop NDAs being abused, saying they were “central” to the problem of enforced silence.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

“I am working closely with colleagues at MoJ [Ministry of Justice],” she said. “I’ve discussed this issue with them over recent days. This will be part of the conversation that we have with the creative industries when I convene the roundtable next week.”

Separate moves, albeit in the slightly longer term, are likely to lead to a law change so that any adult who has penetrative sex with a child aged under 16 would automatically be charged with rape.

Lady Casey has called for swifter action to protect children and young people from high-profile men, and has urged ministers to change the law to close such loopholes.

#207. Lebanon Faces Economic ‘Catastrophe’ After War and Years of Mismanagement

Hezbollah’s conflict with Israel and the U.S.-Israel war with Iran have made systemic problems worse, causing the cost of living to soar and driving many Lebanese to despair.

Reporting from Douris and Beirut, Lebanon

For decades, Abdelnaser Ossman has grown grapes at his family’s expansive farm in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, tilling the soil through years of drought, war and economic turmoil.

But this year the pressures have become overwhelming. His costs have soared and profits have plunged since the war between Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group, began in March. Fuel and fertilizer prices have doubled and labor costs have quintupled, while the price his harvest fetches has dropped by half. Mr. Ossman, 55, has rented out part of his land to help make ends meet and is considering selling parts of his farm.

“This year has been a catastrophe,” he said. “This is the hardest year of them all.”

Lebanon is facing a deepening economic crisis caused by years of mismanagement and exacerbated by a conflict that has killed thousands, displaced hundreds of thousands more and left entire towns in ruins. The U.S.-Israel war with Iran that began in February has only added to the economic challenges.

The data is stark. The World Bank forecasts inflation as rising more than 17 percent in Lebanon this year, driven by supply disruptions, higher shipping costs and soaring fuel prices. It also predicts that the economy will contract by 6.4 percent.

For many Lebanese, economic survival is the overriding concern, as they struggle to afford basic necessities and fuel amid joblessness and low wages. The crisis threatens to derail the fragile progress made by Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who took office last year with ambitions to overhaul the economy. The government faces mounting public anger, unions threatening to strike and growing demands for a lasting overhaul of financial policy.

#206. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#203. Leeds woman, 18, admits knife murder of 16-year-old love rival

Kayla Smith stabbed Chloe Watson Dransfield to death during planned fight over young man

An 18-year-old woman who stabbed a teenage girl to death during a planned fight over a young man has pleaded guilty to murder.

Chloe Watson Dransfield, 16, was attacked by Kayla Smith, 18, after going to the latter’s home with her boyfriend Blake Dowling in Leeds, West Yorkshire, a court heard.

Smith had pleaded guilty to manslaughter but denied murder. She then changed her plea to guilty on the second day of her trial at Leeds crown court on Thursday.

Dowling, 18, who took Chloe to the house, and Archie Rycroft, 20, who followed Smith to the fight on 28 March, are also charged with murder and manslaughter and their trial will continue. They both deny the charges against them.

The judge, Mr Justice Cavanagh KC, said he would sentence Smith when the trial concluded, adding the only sentence he could give was life imprisonment but he would need to set the minimum term she must spend in custody.

The trial previously heard Dowling had been in a relationship with both Chloe and Smith and “knew of the bad feeling between the two females”, although they had never met in person before the fatal attack.

Dowling’s mother told the court Smith was “jealous and obsessed” over her son’s relationship with Chloe.

The prosecution said Chloe and Smith had argued over the phone the previous evening, with Smith threatening to “stab her” several times.

Prior to the attack, Dowling was with Chloe and spoke to Smith on the phone, who was at her grandfather’s house in Austhorpe, east Leeds, with Rycroft.

The court heard a friend of Chloe’s who was on FaceTime with her said she heard Dowling answering his phone and heard Smith screaming: “Blake, I’m gonna smash your head in … you better not be with no girls … Chloe better not be there.”

When Chloe said she was there, the witness heard Smith say: “I’m gonna stab you in your throat.”

The two love rivals agreed to fight and Dowling booked a taxi to take Chloe to Smith’s home.

Giving evidence on Thursday, the friend said that as Chloe was on the way to Smith’s house she told her she was “off to get the fight that I’ve wanted for ages”.

Gill Batts KC, defending Dowling, asked what she thought the fight would entail. The witness replied: “Just themselves, nothing else,” meaning there would be no weapons.

The court was shown CCTV and video doorbell footage which showed Smith emerging from the annexe in her grandfather’s garden holding a knife.

Rycroft followed Smith as she left the property to fight with Chloe who was heard shouting “come on big girl”, and was then seen running back to the annexe with Rycroft after the stabbing.

Chloe, who had been stabbed five times in the neck and back, bled to death.

Prosecutor Mark McKone KC said Rycroft was accused of murder “by walking with Kayla Smith to the fight and by trying to film Kayla Smith using violence and by providing support to her, if needed”.

He added Dowling knew Smith wanted to stab Chloe and by booking the taxi “played a part in organising the violence, assisted and encouraged Kayla Smith by taking Chloe to the scene for the purpose of fighting”.

Smith’s grandfather, Geoff Smith, called for an ambulance 37 minutes after the stabbing and was seen by a neighbour performing CPR on Chloe.

The jury heard Chloe was taken by ambulance to hospital but was pronounced dead at 6.40am.

When police arrested Smith and Rycroft, the prosecution said they were “laughing and joking” with two of their friends and using nitrous oxide in front of officers.

McKone said Dowling denied knowing that Chloe would be caused really serious harm, while Rycroft said he followed Smith out of curiosity and did not see that she had a knife.

#201. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#198. This Defense Makes Drones (and GPS) Think They’re in Peru

GPS-linked devices have been insisting that Ukrainians are in Lima, the Peruvian capital. The culprit is a jamming system built to thwart Russian airstrikes.

Reporting from somewhere in Ukraine. Or Peru.

The S.U.V. in front of us suddenly pulled over. The driver had been trying to lead us to antennas near Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, that scramble the signals of Russian drones and missiles, but his GPS had gone haywire.

“Apologies. Some technical issues,” texted Serhii, a spokesman for Cascade Systems, the Ukrainian defense company that made the system. He asked that only his first name be used, out of concern for his safety.

We should have known: The S.U.V.’s navigation system had decided that the vehicle was in Lima, Peru, 7,628 miles southwest of Kyiv.

This happens all the time to Ukrainians. When Cascade’s antennas are switched on to misdirect Russian bombardments, the GPS in phones and cars is often misdirected, too — to that particular South American city.

This was now happening to a few of the very guys behind the mapping chaos. They had been hoisted on their own antennas, so to speak.

The system, called Lima for obvious reasons, blasts out electromagnetic interference meant to strip the eyes and ears from Moscow’s missiles and drones, making them think they are somewhere else.
